periods.activity_title: Activating Prior Knowledge: Para-athletes and Paralympics

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Reflect and Respond (p.137): observe Sheetal Devi image, discuss and caption
Reflect and Respond (p.138): K-W-L table on Paralympics, paired sharing

time_bands.activity: Open by displaying the image of Sheetal Devi. Ask students to observe carefully and share initial impressions about her posture, equipment, and expression with the class.
Facilitate a whole-class discussion on whether the personality inspires them and why. Elicit varied responses and invite students to suggest a caption for the image.

Distribute or display the K-W-L table from Reflect and Respond (p.138). Students individually complete 'What I Know' and 'What I Want to Know' columns, then share with a partner and discuss as a class.
Teacher reads aloud the opening paragraphs of the informational text (p.137–139) with students following. Pause to clarify unfamiliar terms such as 'locomotor', 'sensory', and 'para-athletics'.

periods.teacher_notes: Students may conflate Paralympics with Special Olympics — clarify that Paralympics is for athletes with physical, sensory, or intellectual impairments competing at elite level. The K-W-L table is a diagnostic tool; accept all prior knowledge without correction at this stage, noting misconceptions to address during reading. Flag the unanchored caption sub-item as a quick oral close if time permits.
materials: Textbook p.137–139 (with image of Sheetal Devi)
Whiteboard or projector for displaying the image
K-W-L table (textbook p.138 or teacher-reproduced on the board)

periods.activity_title: Reading the Interview: Dr. Deepa Malik's Journey and Fact Mapping

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Reading for Meaning (p.143): fact table on Dr. Deepa Malik's diagnosis, surgery, awards, firsts

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads aloud the interview with Dr. Deepa Malik (p.139–143), assigning sections to students in turn. Draw attention to stage directions in the interview format and the interviewer's questions.

Students individually complete the fact table from Reading for Meaning (p.143), filling in details about diagnosis age, surgery outcome, recognition body, breakthrough event, list of firsts, awards, and advocacy areas. Teacher circulates and prompts with guiding questions.

Whole-class discussion to verify and consolidate fact-table entries. Highlight that Dr. Malik's 'two choices' moment (p.143) is the text's turning point and invite students to articulate it in their own words.

periods.teacher_notes: Students often conflate the Arjuna Award with the Khel Ratna; clarify these are distinct national honours referenced in the text. The fact table anchors all seven sub-items — ensure every row is addressed before moving to discussion.
materials: Fact table (textbook p.143 or teacher-reproduced on board)

periods.activity_title: Distinguishing Fact-Opinion and Cause-Effect in the Interview

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Check Your Understanding (p.143–144): identify fact-opinion vs cause-effect in two sentence sets
Check Your Understanding (p.144): paired identification of cause-effect or fact-opinion in two pairs

time_bands.activity: Review the concepts of fact-opinion and cause-effect with brief examples from everyday life. Ask students to give one example of each before opening the textbook.

Students work individually on the two sentence sets from Check Your Understanding (p.143–144), identifying whether each set shows fact-opinion or cause-effect. Teacher facilitates brief sharing after each set.
In pairs, students complete the two pairs from the second task (p.144) and write 1 or 2 in the provided boxes. Pairs compare answers and resolve disagreements before whole-class verification.
Quick whole-class debrief: teacher elicits the key distinction between 'opinion' (belief, interpretation) and 'cause-effect' (consequence), using Dr. Malik's own words from the interview as anchors.

periods.teacher_notes: A common error is labelling any strong statement as 'opinion' — redirect students to test whether the statement can be verified by evidence in the text. Having read the interview, students should be able to locate the factual statements directly in the text. The pair on Dr. Malik's Working Group membership (p.144) often confuses students because 'believed' signals opinion even when paired with a factual sentence.

periods.activity_title: Close Reading of Extracts: Language, Tone, and Meaning

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Critical Reflection (p.145): Extract 1 — caterpillar analogy, breakthrough, hindsight, perceptions
Critical Reflection (p.146): Extract 2 — tone identification, analogy, true-false, push boundaries

time_bands.activity: Teacher reads Extract 1 (p.145) aloud slowly. Students underline any phrase they find striking or unusual before responding.

Students work through all five sub-questions for Extract 1 (p.145) individually, then compare with a neighbour. Teacher facilitates class discussion focusing on the caterpillar-butterfly analogy and the meaning of 'in hindsight'.
Teacher reads Extract 2 (p.146) aloud. Students identify the speaker's tone before attempting the questions.

Students work through all five sub-questions for Extract 2 (p.146). Teacher draws attention to how the phrase 'new lease of life' carries the chapter's central theme. Whole-class discussion closes the unit on both extracts.

periods.teacher_notes: Both extracts must be fully covered in this unit — all five sub-items each. The caterpillar analogy (Extract 1) is interpretive, so accept well-reasoned student formulations that reference personal transformation and the choice to pursue para-athletics. In Extract 2, students often mistake 'moralistic' for the correct tone descriptor; guide them to test each adjective against specific phrases in the extract.
materials: Whiteboard for noting tone options from the MCQ

periods.activity_title: Analytical Extended Responses: Title, Theme, and Life Lessons

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Critical Reflection (p.146–147): extended questions on societal perceptions, title justification, and life lesson

homework.task_brief: Critical Reflection (p.147): extended questions on gender equality, 'ability beyond disability', and personal learning — complete remaining sub-items

time_bands.activity: Brief recap: having completed close reading of both extracts, invite students to articulate in one sentence what they think the chapter's central argument is. Record three or four responses on the board.

Students respond individually in writing to the extended questions on how Dr. Malik's achievements challenge societal perceptions and what long-term impact youth advocacy on disability may have (p.146). Teacher circulates, prompting students to cite evidence from the interview.

Students draft a response to the title-justification question (p.146): 'Rationalise the appropriateness of the title with reference to Dr. Deepa Malik's attitude and achievements.' Volunteers share; teacher models how to structure a title-justification argument.
Assign the remaining extended questions (p.147) as written work to be completed independently. Clarify the depth expected for each response before students leave.

periods.teacher_notes: Title justification is a secondary-stage analytical skill; model the three-part structure — restate the title, link it to a specific moment in the text, then generalise to the chapter's theme. The sub-items on gender equality and 'ability beyond disability' (p.147) are moved to homework because the budget for this unit is fully used by the first three sub-items; flag these as requiring written paragraph responses, not one-line answers.

periods.activity_title: Phrases, Pace, and Modal Auxiliaries in Context

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.147): match five phrases to meanings, then use each in a sentence
Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.148): arrange movement words on pace cline from slowest to fastest
Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.148): match modal verbs to their functions in four sentences

time_bands.activity: Students work in pairs on the phrase-matching task (p.147): match 'defy the odds', 'a new lease of life', 'in hindsight', 'breakthrough moment', and 'turn obstacles into stepping stones' to their meanings. Each pair then writes one original sentence per phrase.

Students arrange the eleven movement words on the pace cline (p.148) from slowest to fastest. Teacher elicits the order on the board, discussing shades of meaning between near-synonyms such as 'saunter', 'stroll', and 'amble'.

Students match modal verbs from four interview sentences to their functions (p.148): 'could' for past ability, 'couldn't' for impossibility, 'should' for obligation, 'would' for prediction. Whole-class verification follows.

Quick consolidation: teacher writes three new sentences on the board using modals in different functions and asks students to identify the function. Connect to how Dr. Malik uses modal language to express possibility and resolve.

periods.teacher_notes: Students frequently confuse 'saunter' and 'stroll' on the cline — both are leisurely, but 'stroll' implies slightly more purposeful movement; allow discussion before settling the order. The phrase-matching task anchors all five entries in the table; ensure students write their own sentences (not copy from the text) so the task doubles as a productive vocabulary exercise. Sub-items on extended modal-function writing (p.149) are not anchored in this unit; flag them as self-study.

periods.activity_title: Direct and Reported Speech: Observation, Rules, and Conversion

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.149–150): identify speech type and sentence type; note changes from direct to reported speech in Column 3
Vocabulary and Structures in Context (p.151): convert Siya–Tarun conversation to reported speech

time_bands.activity: Display two sentences from the interview — one in direct speech, one in reported speech — on the board. Ask students to name the type and identify what has changed: pronouns, tense, and reporting verb.

Students complete the identification task (p.149): label the sentences as direct or reported speech and as declarative, interrogative, exclamatory, or imperative. They then fill Column 3 of the observation table (p.150) for all three sentence pairs, noting changes in tense, pronoun, and conjunction.

Students convert the Siya–Tarun dialogue on para equestrian (p.151) to reported speech, completing all four blanks. Pairs swap notebooks to cross-check tense and pronoun shifts before whole-class review.

Teacher consolidates the three rules students have discovered: tense back-shift, pronoun change, and conjunction insertion. Use one sentence from Dr. Malik's interview to demonstrate all three rules simultaneously.

periods.teacher_notes: Reported-speech errors at secondary level typically involve forgetting to back-shift the present perfect and mishandling first-person pronouns when the reporting verb's subject changes; watch for both during pair work. The Siya–Tarun dialogue (p.151) is grounded in para-equestrian content, which connects naturally to the chapter's Paralympic theme. Sub-item on extended modal writing (p.149) remains unanchored; direct students to it as self-study for consolidation.

periods.activity_title: Listening to an Announcement and Practising Formal and Informal Interviews

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Listen and Respond (p.152): World Inclusion Day assembly announcement — fill five blanks with exact words
Speaking Activity (p.152–153): informal interview of Sports Captain and formal interview of Sports Coach in pairs, roles interchanged

time_bands.activity: Introduce the listening context: students will hear a school announcement for World Inclusion Day. Ask them to predict what details such an announcement might include.

Read the transcript aloud twice at natural pace (teacher uses transcript on p.268). On first listening, students listen only; on second, they fill in all five blanks on p.152 with exact words. Verify answers as a class.

Introduce the interview activity (p.152–153). Discuss what distinguishes formal from informal register — greeting, pronoun use, sentence structure, and level of formality in questions — before students begin.

In pairs, students conduct the informal Sports Captain interview first using the four prompts (p.152), then swap roles for the formal Sports Coach interview (p.153). Teacher circulates, noting register errors for feedback.
Two pairs share one exchange each — one informal, one formal. Class identifies one difference in register between the two performances.

periods.teacher_notes: For the listening task, read the transcript at a natural but measured pace; a second reading allows students who missed a word to catch up. The key error in the interview activity is students using the same register for both contexts — emphasise before they begin that 'Could you tell me…' and 'Tell me about…' signal different relationships. The listening task's five blanks all have exact-word answers verifiable from the transcript.
materials: Transcript text (teacher copy, p.268 of transcript appendix)

periods.activity_title: Drafting a Notice and Planning a Paralympic Presentation

tasks_in_class.task_brief: Writing Task (p.154): draft a 50-word notice in a box for Inter-school Athletic Meet registrations
Learning Beyond the Text (p.154): form groups and plan a presentation on two lesser-known Paralympic sports or two Indian Paralympians

time_bands.activity: Review the structural elements of a notice — Name of Organisation, NOTICE heading, date, body, signature, designation — and the 50-word ceiling. Display a brief model notice on the board, distinct from the textbook's scenario.

Students individually draft their notice (p.154) in their notebooks, drawing a box around it. Teacher circulates and gives formative feedback on format adherence, word count, and essential details. Students revise on the spot before a final version is written.
Two or three students read their notices aloud. Class evaluates: does the notice include all eight required elements? Is it within the word limit? Teacher confirms or corrects.

Introduce the group presentation project (p.154): groups of four choose one topic — two lesser-known Paralympic sports or two Indian Paralympians — and plan their slide structure (introductory slide, origin slides, topic slides, concluding slide). Groups decide roles and note initial research questions.
Groups briefly state their chosen topic and one key question they will research. Teacher notes group compositions on the board and clarifies research sources: magazines, newspapers, and internet.

periods.teacher_notes: The notice task must be completed and revised within the unit — drafting, peer response, and final version all happen here, since the writing task is planned to begin and end inside a single unit. For the presentation project, groups should leave with a clear division of roles and at least one agreed research question; the platform will not serve another unit to continue from where this one ends. Students who have read about the Paralympic history in the 'Did you know?' section (p.154) will have a head start on the origin slides.
materials: Student notebooks and rulers (for drawing the notice box)
Whiteboard for notice-element checklist and group-topic record

items.source_context: Dr. Deepa Malik's choice between remorse and para-athletics, her Rio silver medal, and her advocacy for disability rights.
items.item_stem:
Read the following statements about Dr. Deepa Malik. Decide whether each statement is TRUE or FALSE and give a one-sentence reason from the interview text.
(1) Dr. Malik was already practising athletics when she was diagnosed with the spinal tumour.
(2) Her silver medal at the 2016 Rio Paralympic Games was also historically significant as India's first female Paralympic medal.
(3) Dr. Malik believes that Paralympics can change public attitudes towards disability.

options.text: Dr. Malik believes that Paralympics can change public attitudes towards disability.
Dr. Malik was already practising athletics when she was diagnosed with the spinal tumour.
Her silver medal at the 2016 Rio Paralympic Games was also historically significant as India's first female Paralympic medal.

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: 1. FALSE — Dr. Malik was a swimmer before her diagnosis; she transitioned to para-athletics only after her surgery and permanent paralysis. 2. TRUE — the text states she is India's first female Paralympic medallist across any sport. 3. TRUE — she explicitly states Paralympics has 'the extraordinary ability to challenge stereotypes and change attitudes towards disability'.

items.source_lo: Student analyses an informational interview text by distinguishing fact from opinion, identifying cause-effect relationships, evaluating language and tone in extracts, and constructing analytical responses on theme, title, and societal impact using informational prose as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Dr. Deepa Malik's choice between remorse and para-athletics, her Rio silver medal, and her advocacy for disability rights.
items.item_stem:
Read the passage above and answer the questions that follow.

1. What are the “preconceived notions” Dr. Malik refers to, and about whom are they held?
2. According to the passage, what causes people’s attitudes towards disability to change? State the cause and its effect in Dr. Malik’s argument.
3. Dr. Malik says the Paralympics “has given me a new lease of life”. Explain what this phrase means, in the light of the journey she describes in the first extract.
4. The text is titled ‘The World of Limitless Possibilities’. Using this passage — including what she says about having been a swimmer — explain how well that title captures Dr. Malik’s outlook.
items.visual_stimulus:
From the interview (p.145):
“1. I love sports and had been a swimmer too, so I decided to switch to para-athletics. This is how my Paralympics journey began. My breakthrough moment came in the 2016 Rio Paralympic Games, when I secured the silver medal in the shot-put event. In hindsight, I feel it was a moment of personal victory and a step forward in changing perceptions.
2. Honestly, I feel sports, especially Paralympics, have the extraordinary ability to challenge stereotypes and change attitudes towards disability. When people witness the strength, skill, and competitive spirit of para-athletes, it breaks down preconceived notions. Paralympics has given me a new lease of life and helped me push boundaries.”

expected_elements: Identifies 'preconceived notions' as stereotypes about disabled people's capabilities.
Explains that witnessing para-athletes' competitive spirit is the stated cause of attitude change.
Links 'new lease of life' to Dr. Malik's personal transformation from paralysis to achievement.
Evaluates the title: 'limitless possibilities' mirrors the journey the first extract describes — swimmer to Paralympic medallist — and her philosophy of ability beyond disability.
Discusses how Dr. Malik's prior swimming experience made her transition to para-athletics achievable, not accidental.

items.item_stem:
Listen to the World Inclusion Day assembly announcement. Then answer the following questions by selecting the correct option.
(1) On which occasion is the special assembly being held?
(2) Who delivers the welcome speech at the start of the assembly?
(3) Which student group stages a presentation on inclusion?

what_each_option_reveals.A: Student may have confused 'Inclusion' with the more familiar 'Disability Awareness' framing.
what_each_option_reveals.D: Student may have associated the assembly with the chapter's sport theme rather than the announcement's stated occasion.
what_each_option_reveals.B: Student may have overgeneralised from wellness or community-event associations.

items.item_stem: After listening to the World Inclusion Day announcement, reflect on the following: The announcement describes the assembly as ending with a song 'to nurture inclusive practices and collaboration'. In two or three sentences, explain what the choice of ending with a song — rather than, say, a speech — suggests about the organisers' view of how inclusion is best promoted within a school community.

expected_elements: Notes that a song is a participatory, collective act rather than one-way communication.
Links the choice of song to the theme of collaboration mentioned in the announcement.
Suggests the organisers believe shared experience builds inclusion more effectively than instruction.
Connects the emotional or affective quality of music to nurturing community bonds.

items.item_stem: You are interviewing a classmate who is playing the role of a para-athlete who recently represented your state in a national competition. Conduct an informal interview of at least four exchanges. Ask about their sporting journey, a challenge they overcame, and what message they have for others. Speak naturally and respond to what your partner says, not just to a prepared script.

expected_elements: Uses informal register: contractions, first-name address, conversational phrasing.
Asks follow-up questions that respond to the interviewee's actual answers.
Covers all three areas: sporting journey, challenge overcome, message for others.
Listens actively — does not read from a script or ignore the partner's response.
Maintains natural turn-taking across at least four exchanges.

items.source_lo: Student conducts and participates in both formal and informal interview exchanges, adapting register, question framing, and response style to different communicative contexts using role-based speaking as the vehicle.

items.item_stem: Your school is considering abolishing the annual sports day to give more time to academic preparation. Argue either for or against this proposal in a formal group discussion of four students. Use specific reasons and at least one piece of evidence or example to support your position, and respond directly to at least one point made by another speaker.

expected_elements: Takes a clear position and states it explicitly at the outset.
Provides at least one specific reason supported by an example or evidence.
Uses formal register: complete sentences, no slang, appropriate address.
Responds directly to a point raised by another speaker, agreeing or disagreeing with reasons.
Contributes to a genuine exchange rather than delivering a monologue.

Present your notice within a box and include all required format elements.

Register is formal and appropriate for an institutional announcement.

Write a letter to the editor of your school newsletter (120–150 words) arguing that your school should introduce a dedicated weekly period for students to learn about para-sports and disability inclusion. Give at least two reasons and use a persuasive tone throughout.

items.item_stem: Match each phrase from Column A with its correct meaning in Column B.
items.visual_stimulus:
Column A | Column B
defy the odds | (i) a time of significant development or discovery
a new lease of life | (ii) overcome challenges and achieve goals
in hindsight | (iii) succeed when most people expected failure
breakthrough moment | (iv) ability to understand something after it has happened
turn obstacles into stepping stones | (v) become more energetic and active than before

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: defy the odds — (iii); a new lease of life — (v); in hindsight — (iv); breakthrough moment — (i); turn obstacles into stepping stones — (ii)

answer_key.right: (iii) succeed when most people expected failure
(v) become more energetic and active than before
(iv) ability to understand something after it has happened
(i) a time of significant development or discovery

items.item_stem:
Rewrite the following sentences from the interview in reported speech. Pay careful attention to changes in tense, pronouns, and conjunctions.
(1) Dr. Malik said, "I believe youth is the voice of tomorrow."
(2) The interviewer asked, "Did you face any resistance from society?"
(3) Dr. Malik declared, "I will continue to advocate for the rights of persons with disabilities."

teacher_guide.suggested_answer: (1) Dr. Malik said that she believed youth was the voice of tomorrow. (2) The interviewer asked whether she had faced any resistance from society. (3) Dr. Malik declared that she would continue to advocate for the rights of persons with disabilities.

items.item_stem: The Paralympic movement champions the philosophy that disability is not a limitation but a unique strength. In a well-developed paragraph of 80–100 words, explain what you understand by this philosophy and give one example — from the text or from your own knowledge — that illustrates it.

expected_elements: Articulates the core idea: disability does not define a person's potential.
Uses a specific example, either Dr. Malik's journey or another para-athlete.
Explains how the example illustrates the philosophy, not just describes it.
Writes in well-structured prose with a clear topic and concluding sentence.
Stays within the word limit and uses formal academic register.

items.source_lo: Student conducts independent research and collaboratively designs a structured multi-slide presentation on a disability-sports topic, integrating information from multiple sources and presenting findings to an audience using project-work as the vehicle.
items.source_context: Group research on lesser-known Paralympic sports or Indian Paralympians, structured as a multi-slide class presentation.
items.item_stem:
In a group of three or four, research ONE of the following topics and prepare a presentation of six to eight slides to share with the class:
(a) Two para-sports that are not widely known in India — cover the rules, equipment, and why these sports are significant for inclusion.
(b) Two Indian Paralympians (other than Dr. Deepa Malik) — cover their sporting discipline, key achievements, and the barriers they overcame.
Your presentation must include: one introductory slide, slides on the history of the Paralympic movement, slides on your chosen topic, and one concluding slide. Each group member must present at least one slide. Use a mix of text and images, and cite your sources on the final slide.

expected_elements: Covers both required subjects (two sports or two athletes) with factual accuracy.
Follows the prescribed slide structure: intro, history, topic slides, conclusion.
Balances text and images; does not overload slides with dense paragraphs.
Every group member presents at least one slide confidently.
Sources are cited and research draws on at least two different types of reference.
